slides.title: A home vector survives a winding outward journey
body: **Path integration** is the continual updating of direction and distance from a starting point using information gathered during movement. A **home vector** specifies the direction and distance back to the nest; it need not reproduce the sequence of outward turns.

Müller and Wehner recorded a natural foraging trip of Cataglyphis fortis in Tunisia. The outward path measured 354.5 m, while the maximum distance from the nest was 113.2 m. After finding food, the ant returned along a comparatively direct inbound route.

The difference between outward path length and nest displacement separates route retracing from vector-guided homing. This recorded journey documents the behavior, but does not identify a neuron that stores the vector or establish the mathematical precision of its updating mechanism.

slides.title: Displacement separates the vector from the real nest
body: Passive displacement changes an ant’s geographical position without supplying the walking movements that normally update its home vector. A displaced ant can therefore express a direction appropriate to its earlier position rather than to the nest’s actual location.

Müller and Wehner captured a food-carrying ant at its feeding location and released it elsewhere in open terrain. The animal’s subsequent course was compared with the geographical nest direction and the course predicted from its recorded outbound trajectory, using a 10 m spatial scale.

The course retained information from the outward journey despite the transfer. The test distinguishes movement-derived navigation from immediate attraction to the true nest, while leaving landmark guidance and systematic searching available as additional mechanisms under natural conditions.

slides.title: Angular channels constrain the path being integrated
body: An experimental path can specify the directions and distances an ant experiences before homing. Müller and Wehner trained Cataglyphis fortis through narrow plastic channels, then transferred individuals from the feeder to a separate open test field.

The two legs were varied over lengths of 5–10 m and turning angles spanning 0–180°. In the plotted experiment, the first leg was 10 m and the second 5 m. Release occurred within one minute of capture, reducing the delay between training and the directional test.

The recorded initial homeward course measures the ant’s accumulated directional estimate rather than its ability to follow the training channel backward. Removing the channels during testing separates the geometry experienced during acquisition from the geometry available during expression.

slides.title: Homing errors depend on the outward turning angle
body: **Systematic error** means a directional deviation that varies predictably with an experimental manipulation. It differs from random scatter among journeys. Müller and Wehner measured the angular difference between the true homeward direction and the course expressed after two-leg training.

With outbound legs of 10 m and 5 m, the error increased as the turning angle approached approximately 150°, reaching about 20° in the published measurements. The error returned toward zero at the limiting straight or reversed arrangements.

The angle-dependent pattern supported an approximate updating rule under these conditions. It does not prove that every ant species, every route geometry, or every neural representation uses the same approximation; the inference concerns the measured Cataglyphis trajectories and their proposed mathematical account.

slides.title: Sun and polarization cues support the directional test
body: A **celestial compass** derives heading information from features of the sky. Direct sunlight and the pattern of polarized skylight provide related but separable information. Polarization refers to the orientation of the electric field oscillation in a light wave.

Müller and Wehner compared homing errors while ants used the sun, polarized skylight, or both. Screening the sun removed direct solar information; painting the dorsal rim of the compound eyes removed access to the specialized polarization-sensitive eye region. The 10 m and 5 m route still produced systematic errors.

The persistence of the error pattern across compass conditions argues against a single defective sky cue accounting for the path-integration bias. Restricted sky windows can themselves distort polarization estimates, so the authors considered this separate source of compass error in their interpretation.

slides.title: Three-leg routes test an approximate updating rule
body: An explanation fitted to one route geometry must also account for a different sequence of movements. Müller and Wehner added a third leg to the channel arrangement, introducing a second 90° turn rather than repeating the original two-leg experiment.

The first leg was 10 m and the second and third legs were each 5 m. Ants subsequently released into open terrain deviated by 30.8° from the true home direction. The approximation derived from the earlier experiments predicted a deviation of 33.7°.

The agreement extended the behavioral account beyond the particular angles used to derive it. A successful prediction of homing direction still leaves the cellular implementation unresolved: the experiment measured the animal’s course, not the voltage, transmitter or synaptic activity of an identified integrator.

slides.title: Natural routes can limit the cost of directional bias
body: Route geometry determines how an approximate path integrator accumulates error. A sharp sustained turn can produce a large deviation, whereas turns in opposite directions may partly cancel their effects on the estimated homeward direction.

Müller and Wehner compared the proposed updating rule with recorded natural foraging paths. In the displaced example, the expressed course departed from the real nest direction by approximately 20°, consistent with the direction predicted from that ant’s outward trajectory.

The authors noted that natural Cataglyphis paths rarely contained the repeated sharp backward turns that generated especially large experimental errors. This ecological interpretation explains possible usefulness without establishing perfect accuracy; landmarks and searching remain relevant when a home vector is insufficient.

slides.title: Leg length manipulation changes the estimated distance
body: An **odometer** is a mechanism for estimating distance traveled. A **stride** is one complete movement cycle of a particular leg. Altering leg length can change the distance covered during each stride without changing the distance experienced before the manipulation.

Wittlinger and colleagues trained Cataglyphis fortis to a feeder 10 m from the nest. At the feeder, they lengthened legs with attached pig bristles, producing stilts, or shortened legs, producing stumps. Food-carrying ants were then tested in a separate channel.

The manipulation was performed after the outbound distance had been acquired, allowing an unequal relationship between outbound and inbound strides. The resulting distance error tests locomotor information, but leg surgery alone does not distinguish peripheral sensory feedback from centrally generated movement signals.

slides.title: Stilts overshoot and stumps undershoot the nest
body: The transition from directed walking to repeated U-turns provides a behavioral measure of expected nest distance. Wittlinger and colleagues used the median of the initial six turning points to identify the centre of an ant’s nest-search behavior.

After a normal 10 m outbound journey, ants with lengthened legs searched at 15.30 m, ants with shortened legs searched at 5.75 m, and normal-legged controls searched at 10.20 m. The direction of the error followed the change in stride length.

Longer inbound strides made the stored journey terminate farther from release, while shorter strides made it terminate sooner. This bidirectional effect is difficult to attribute solely to debilitation, which would not predict vigorous overshooting by the animals walking on stilts.

slides.title: Matched outward and inward legs restore homing distance
body: The same modified animal can experience a new outbound journey with the altered legs. This control keeps the manipulation present while removing the mismatch between the locomotor conditions used to acquire and express the stored distance.

After returning to the nest, ants walked to the feeder again with their stilts or stumps and were retested. Searches centred at 10.55 m for stilts and 10.25 m for stumps, close to the 10.20 m normal-leg condition and the true 10 m separation.

Recovery of the expected distance supports a stride-dependent acquisition-and-readout relationship rather than permanent loss of navigation after surgery. It does not require the ant to measure its leg length explicitly or identify which neural signal constitutes the odometer’s input.

slides.title: Two shortening treatments separate locomotor effects
body: Wittlinger and colleagues extended the odometer experiment with two degrees of leg shortening. **Tarsomeres** are the distal segments of an insect leg; the **tibia** lies proximal to the tarsus. Removing these regions changes the effective length of the walking limb.

Stumps I lacked the distal tarsal segments, whereas stumps II had the distal half of the tibia removed. A third group carried bristle stilts, and normal-legged ants provided the comparison. All groups had acquired the same 10 m outbound feeder distance before the first test.

The anatomically graded manipulation allowed comparison of different reductions in stride length rather than treating all shortened legs as one condition. It preserved a common navigational task, while acknowledging that leg length, walking speed and load can change together.

slides.title: Shortened legs retain alternating tripod coordination
body: A **tripod gait** alternates two sets of three supporting legs. In Cataglyphis, one set combines the left front and hind legs with the right middle leg; the complementary set uses the remaining three legs.

High-speed video at 250 frames per second recorded ants before and after manipulation. The published normal example had a stride length of 13.3 mm at 0.28 m/s, whereas a stumps-II example retained tripod coordination with a 10.5 mm stride at 0.27 m/s.

The observations separate shortening of the walking cycle’s spatial extent from replacement of its basic coordination pattern. Preserved tripods do not establish unchanged sensory feedback or motor-neuron activity, but they constrain explanations that require an entirely different gait after shortening.

slides.title: Distance errors track the extent of leg shortening
body: A shorter stride covers less ground during each locomotor cycle. If outbound distance is stored in relation to movement cycles, shortening the legs only after that journey should make the inbound estimate terminate before the original feeder-to-nest distance.

In the expanded experiment, normal-legged ants searched at 10.20 m, stumps-I ants at 6.95 m and stumps-II ants at 5.75 m. Stilts produced searches at 15.30 m. These values were measured after a 10 m outbound run through the training channel.

The graded undershoot is consistent with a stride integrator rather than a fixed physical-distance readout independent of locomotion. The two shortening treatments nevertheless changed more than one biomechanical variable, so recorded stride kinematics were needed to assess the quantitative prediction.

slides.title: Search density distinguishes distance from uncertainty
body: A **search density distribution** records how often an ant visits positions during its search. Its centre estimates expected nest location, while its width describes how broadly the animal distributes its search around that estimate.

The test channel was divided into 10 cm bins. In the first test, the full width at half maximum was 8.3 m for stilts, 6.0 m for normal legs, 5.2 m for stumps I and 4.1 m for stumps II. The plotted search curves therefore differed in spread as well as centre.

The widths are behavioral descriptions of searching rather than direct measurements of a neural uncertainty variable. Longer or shorter strides alter the spatial extent covered during searching, so distribution width cannot by itself establish how precisely a central memory encodes distance.

slides.title: Repeated training removes most of the distance mismatch
body: Comparing first and second tests separates a newly imposed mismatch from walking with altered legs on both journey directions. In the second test, ants had left the nest and reached the feeder using the same modified limbs used during homing.

The initial stilt and stump searches were displaced from the 10 m nest distance. After the subsequent outbound journey, the color-coded search distributions clustered near the correct distance across the four leg conditions, even though the surgical or bristle modifications remained present.

The dependence on journey history makes a persistent injury explanation insufficient. Matched locomotor conditions permit accurate homing without proving a numerical step counter; a physiological integrator of stride-associated signals can produce the same qualitative relationship between acquisition and return.

slides.title: Body size must be separated from stride length
body: Larger Cataglyphis workers have longer legs and can take longer strides. **Normalization** expresses measurements relative to a specified reference so that differences in body size do not masquerade as effects of the experimental manipulation.

Wittlinger and colleagues measured the **alitrunk**, the thoracic region between the pronotum and propodeum, and expressed middle-leg length and stride length relative to alitrunk length. High-speed records related these relative strides to frequency, including a comparison at 20 Hz.

The analysis placed normal, stilt and stump animals on a common anatomical and locomotor basis. Relative stride length is therefore dimensionless in the relevant plot; it is not a second independently measured estimate of homing distance or evidence that ants themselves perform this normalization.

slides.title: Stride length varies even at a common cycle frequency
body: **Stride frequency** is the number of complete leg cycles per second, measured in hertz. It is distinct from stride length, the distance advanced during one cycle. Either variable can change walking speed.

At comparable frequencies, stilt ants had longer relative strides and stump ants shorter relative strides than controls. The investigators used the measured frequency–length relationships to compare animals at 20 Hz, reducing the effect of unequal movement speeds on the predicted homing distances.

The remaining ordering of the leg conditions links the imposed limb geometry to locomotor displacement. The measured relationships provide a quantitative behavioral constraint, but they do not reveal whether the odometer receives cycle counts, proprioceptive signals or an integrated motor command.

slides.title: Walking speed is not determined by frequency alone
body: Increasing walking speed can involve faster cycles, longer strides, or both. Wittlinger and colleagues recorded freely walking animals under several temperature and preparation conditions, retaining straight runs without abrupt stops for the kinematic comparisons.

The color-coded data related walking speed, in mm/s, to stride frequency, in Hz. Normal and shortened-leg ants increased cycle frequency as speed increased, while stilts tended to use lower frequencies for a given speed. Their longer strides partly compensated for the reduced frequency.

These relationships prevent interpreting every change in elapsed journey time as a proportional change in distance. A time-based explanation must account for the actual measured speeds rather than assume that all manipulated ants maintain the same cycle rate or velocity.

slides.title: Stride length also increases with walking speed
body: The distance advanced during one stride is not a fixed constant for a leg condition. Cataglyphis changes stride length as it runs faster, so the effect of altered limb length must be evaluated across measured locomotor speeds.

The published plot relates stride length in mm to walking speed in mm/s. Stilts have longer strides than controls at comparable speeds, and stumps shorter strides. High-speed recordings establish this relationship independently of the turning-point measures used to locate each ant’s nest search.

The agreement between locomotor displacement and homing bias supports stride-based odometry while avoiding an assumption of one unchanging step size. The measurements still leave unresolved how stride-length information is represented and combined with heading information in the nervous system.

slides.title: A stride integrator need not be a literal counter
body: A **stride integrator** accumulates information associated with rhythmic locomotion. It need not register each footfall as a discrete counted object. Possible inputs include **proprioception**, sensory information about limb position and movement, or activity associated with generating the walking rhythm.

The 2007 experiments combined a 10 m navigational task with 250-frame-per-second video and leg-length manipulations. Both the preserved tripod pattern and the graded stride changes were consistent with accumulation of movement-linked information rather than a fixed elapsed-time rule.

The physiological alternatives were not directly recorded or selectively blocked in this study. No transmitter, receptor or ion channel was identified as the odometer mechanism, so these candidates remain proposed explanations rather than established cellular findings in Cataglyphis.

slides.title: Learning walks precede long-distance foraging
body: **Learning walks** are short excursions around the nest during the transition from interior work to outside foraging. Cataglyphis nodus repeatedly pauses and rotates during these walks, acquiring experience with directional and visual information before taking distant journeys.

It tests experience-dependent structural change; it does not directly measure a complete home vector in an identified neuron or establish each novice’s later foraging success.

slides.title: Sky polarization supplies a changing compass reference
body: The **solar ephemeris** is the sun’s changing position over the day. A time-compensated sky compass must relate current solar or polarization information to heading despite that movement. Initial learning can establish the relation between celestial changes and stable surroundings.

Grob and colleagues compared natural skylight with a stationary polarizer, a single 90° turn at solar noon, hourly 45° turns, and continuous rotation at 15° per hour. Each treatment constrained how polarization direction changed during three days of learning walks.

The artificial schedules separated exposure to polarized light from experience of a changing polarization pattern. They were controlled experimental cues rather than claims that the natural sky everywhere follows those exact angular steps, especially near noon or at different geographical positions.

slides.title: Two visual pathways reach different integration centres
body: A **neuropil** is a region containing neuronal processes and synapses. The **central complex** comprises midline brain neuropils implicated in heading and navigation, while the **mushroom bodies** are paired structures implicated in memory-based processing.

Grob and colleagues labelled Cataglyphis brains with anti-synapsin antibodies and fluorescent phalloidin, which marks actin-rich structures. Their preparations identified mushroom-body collar microglomeruli and giant synapses in the lateral complex. The whole-brain image has a 200 µm scale bar and the synaptic insets 10 µm bars.

The anatomical distinction permits separate measurements along the two visual pathways. Labelling synaptic structures establishes their position and morphology, but neither stain reports the sign of a postsynaptic voltage change, an active compass heading or a stored navigational distance.

slides.title: Synaptic labels distinguish boutons from target processes
body: **Synapsin** is a protein associated with presynaptic vesicles, so anti-synapsin labelling helps identify presynaptic specializations. **F-actin** is filamentous actin; fluorescent phalloidin labels it in neuronal processes and supports identification of synaptic organization.

The Cataglyphis nodus preparations used complementary synapsin and actin labels to quantify **microglomeruli**, compact synaptic complexes in the mushroom-body collar, and giant synapses in the lateral complex. The magnified examples retain 10 µm scale bars for these different structures.

Structural counts can reveal experience-associated reorganization, but an additional labelled complex does not automatically imply increased firing or stronger transmission. The experiments did not measure release probability, receptor conductance or excitatory and inhibitory currents in the counted synapses.

slides.title: Light exposure changes the lateral-complex pathway
body: **Light exposure** and active learning walks are separable experimental experiences. Grob and colleagues compared dark controls with ants exposed to natural skylight, ultraviolet-filtered skylight or a fixed polarization pattern, with additional groups allowed to perform learning walks.

After three days, lateral-complex giant-synapse counts increased under suitable full-spectrum light exposure even without learning walks. Removing ultraviolet light reduced this response. Central-complex volume did not exhibit the same simple light-exposure dependence as the lateral-complex synaptic count.

The dissociation supports different experience requirements in the two visual pathways. It does not identify ultraviolet phototransduction channels or prove that additional lateral-complex synapses are sufficient for accurate homing; the measured endpoint was synaptic structure rather than navigational performance.

slides.title: Central-complex growth requires more than light alone
body: **Structural plasticity** is an experience-associated change in neuronal anatomy, such as neuropil volume or synaptic organization. It must be distinguished from an acute firing-rate response to a sensory stimulus.

After three days, natural learning walks increased the size-corrected central-complex volume relative to dark controls. Passive light exposure and learning walks under a stationary polarization filter did not produce the same increase. Brain volumes were corrected for body size rather than compared solely as raw tissue amounts.

The result links active experience with changing celestial information to central-complex structure. It does not establish whether volume changes arise from extra synapses, expanded neurites or other tissue components, nor whether the observed growth is causally required for path integration.

slides.title: Rotation during learning changes mushroom-body structure
body: The **mushroom-body collar** is a visual input region of the mushroom-body calyx. Its microglomeruli receive visual information and provide a measurable synaptic endpoint for changes accompanying the acquisition of outdoor experience.

Grob and colleagues allowed three days of learning walks under different polarization schedules. A stationary pattern failed to elicit the growth associated with changing polarization. A single 90° daily turn, hourly 45° turns and continuous 15°-per-hour rotation supported increases in collar volume and microglomerular number.

slides.title: Rotation affects higher centres more than giant synapses
body: A common sensory manipulation can affect different brain regions differently. The lateral complex lies along the sky-compass pathway, whereas the central complex and mushroom-body collar provide distinct higher-order measures of experience-associated change.

The continuous rotation condition changed filter orientation at 15° per hour.

The dissociation limits a claim of uniform growth throughout the visual system. Similar giant-synapse numbers do not establish identical activity in that pathway; transmitter release, synaptic strength and firing patterns were not measured by counting anatomical complexes.

slides.title: Transmitter assignments constrain proposed circuit roles
body: **GABAergic** neurons use gamma-aminobutyric acid as a transmitter; **cholinergic** neurons use acetylcholine. These transmitter classifications describe signaling identity, while the postsynaptic effect also depends on receptor type and cellular conditions.

Grob and colleagues discuss evidence that most tangential neurons projecting from the lateral complex toward the central complex are GABAergic, whereas visual projection neurons supplying mushroom bodies are presumably cholinergic. Their three-day experience experiment measured structural endpoints in these pathways rather than pharmacologically isolating transmitter action.

The different transmitter identities may contribute to different plasticity patterns, but that explanation was proposed rather than tested here. The study does not establish which GABA or acetylcholine receptor subtype, ion channel or intracellular cascade causes the observed volume and synaptic changes.

slides.title: Magnetic coils isolate the reference used during learning
body: The **geomagnetic field** is Earth’s magnetic field, which can provide a directional reference independent of the sun’s daily movement. A **Helmholtz coil system** generates controlled magnetic fields in an experimental volume.

Grob and colleagues installed a three-dimensional coil system around a 60 × 60 cm platform connected to a Cataglyphis nodus nest. Novices performed learning walks over three consecutive days. At the site, the natural total field was about 46.1 µT, with a horizontal component of 26.6 µT.

The preparation manipulated magnetic information while retaining the natural panorama and celestial environment. Comparing several magnetic conditions with dark interior-worker controls allowed assessment of experience-associated brain changes, but did not directly identify a magnetic receptor or selectively stimulate a known magnetosensory neuron.

slides.title: Removing horizontal magnetic information disrupts gazes
body: A **pirouette** is a rotation around the ant’s body axis during a learning walk. Under natural conditions, the longest pauses in these rotations are directed toward the nest, providing a measurable orientation behavior near the nest entrance.

In the horizontal-elimination condition, the coils cancelled the horizontal field component while retaining a downward vertical field of about 37.5 µT. The longest stopping directions no longer clustered toward the nest in the published angular distributions, which used 10° bins.

The result supports a role for horizontal magnetic information in the novices’ nest-directed behavior under this condition. It does not prove that every other compass cue is unavailable, and the remaining vertical field differs fundamentally from removing magnetic information entirely.

slides.title: Complete field elimination permits a different outcome
body: Complete magnetic-field elimination is a distinct cue manipulation from retaining a vertical field. Grob and colleagues cancelled both the horizontal and vertical components rather than leaving a directional magnetic cue pointing downward.

Under total elimination, the residual field was about 0.1 µT. Ants nevertheless directed their longest pirouette pauses toward the nest. This differed from the loss of nest-directed gazes when only the horizontal component had been eliminated.

The authors interpreted the contrast as possible recruitment of a backup compass when magnetic information was absent altogether. Panoramic information is a candidate, but the experiment did not independently remove it, so the specific substitute cue and the switching mechanism remain unresolved.

slides.title: A rotating magnetic vector can still guide look-backs
body: A magnetic cue need not always point toward natural magnetic north to provide a usable short-term directional reference. The relevant comparison is whether its direction remains sufficiently stable during each individual learning walk.

In the magnetic-plus-solar condition, the horizontal vector was adjusted every 10 seconds to follow the sun’s azimuth over the day. Individual walks lasted seconds to minutes, and ants retained nest-directed longest stops despite the vector’s changing geographical alignment.

The preservation of look-back behavior does not establish normal long-term calibration. The manipulation makes magnetic and celestial directions covary over the day, removing their natural changing angular relationship even while leaving a useful reference for an individual short excursion.

body: **Compass calibration** establishes the relationship between a sensory directional cue and an internal heading reference. The sun and polarization pattern change over the day, whereas natural magnetic direction and a fixed panorama provide comparatively stable external references.

The candidate contribution of the antennal Johnston’s organ to magnetoreception likewise remains unproven; no magnetic receptor molecule or ion channel was identified.

slides.title: A new route can emerge from familiar goal vectors
body: A **goal vector** specifies a remembered direction and distance to a destination relative to the nest. A **shortcut** connects familiar destinations along a route that was not itself used during training; this behavior need not uniquely imply a metric cognitive map.

Voegeli and colleagues trained Cataglyphis ants to feeders A and B in separate channels. The nest distances were 4.5 m and 5.7 m, and the test channel connected the feeder positions across a 4.1 m separation. Only one nest-channel entrance was open at a time.

slides.title: Alternating training establishes two separate destinations
body: Experience with more than one food source can establish alternative navigational goals. In the channel experiment, feeders were hidden below the channel floor, preventing an approaching ant from simply steering toward a visible food cup.

Ants completed ten training journeys: four to feeder A, four to B and two final journeys to A. Feeder B lay 45° to the left or right of A as viewed from the nest. The subsequent test removed food and opened the connecting test channel at A.

The final visits standardized the starting goal while preserving experience with the second destination. Channel shutters constrained which route was available, but the design still allows the ant to choose search directions within the connecting channel rather than forcing a particular first turn.

slides.title: One-feeder training produces a symmetric local search
body: A one-feeder control establishes the search pattern expected without memory of a second food source. This comparison distinguishes a general tendency to widen a search from a directional bias toward another learned destination.

Control ants visited only feeder A before testing. After food removal, their searches were concentrated around the former feeder position and distributed approximately symmetrically on its two sides. Distance from the starting point was measured in metres along the connecting test channel.

The symmetric baseline constrains interpretations of the two-feeder experiments. A later directional shift cannot be attributed simply to entering that channel, although a density distribution still describes where ants search rather than directly measuring the neural representation of a food vector.

slides.title: Two-feeder experience biases the first search direction
body: The first U-turn after the missing feeder measures an early component of search direction. It is distinct from the full spatial distribution accumulated during later back-and-forth movements in the test channel.

After training to A and B, about two-thirds of the ants made their first U-turn on the side containing the second feeder. The effect occurred with feeder B either left or right of A, whose trained positions were separated by 4.1 m.

The left–right comparison argues against an intrinsic turning preference accounting for the result. The early bias is consistent with using an alternative learned goal, but a first turn alone does not establish arrival accuracy or distinguish all possible computations involving current and remembered vectors.

slides.title: Search expands preferentially toward the missing goal
body: The full search trajectory contains information beyond its first movement. Ants can begin at the expected position of one feeder, then redistribute their efforts toward another destination when the first food source is absent.

Two-feeder ants initially searched around A but progressively widened their searches toward B. Their search-density distributions were asymmetric in the direction of the second feeder, whereas the one-feeder controls were symmetric. The effect reversed when B changed from the left to the right side.

The evidence supports flexible use of prior destination experience without requiring prior travel along A-to-B. It does not demonstrate a landmark-based representation of the connecting space, because the channel experiment was designed around controlled routes and stored vector information.

slides.title: Restricted sky views predict biases in goal searches
body: A narrow channel restricts the visible portion of the polarization pattern. Depending on channel orientation and solar position, this restriction can bias the compass information used during outbound acquisition and therefore alter a stored goal vector.

Voegeli and colleagues separated tests into conditions predicting underestimation or overestimation of the 4.1 m A-to-B distance. Relative search distributions were obtained by subtracting the one-feeder baseline from the two-feeder distributions. Their positive regions shifted in the predicted direction.

The relationship links the searches to compass information acquired through the channels rather than merely to the physical location of an absent feeder. The subtraction is an analysis of recorded behavior, not proof that ants themselves subtract search distributions or represent their uncertainty in this format.

slides.title: Stored goals can interact with the current home vector
body: The **current vector** is updated during ongoing travel, whereas a stored goal vector can persist across journeys. A goal can be approached by comparing the current nest-relative state with a remembered destination rather than constructing a map of all familiar places.

In the two-feeder experiment, ants searched toward B from A along an untrained connecting route separated by 4.1 m. The authors proposed retrieval of B’s food vector into working memory while the path integrator continued to track the ant’s current state.

This account explains the shortcut without requiring a metric cognitive map. It remains an interpretation of behavioral results: the experiment did not record a working-memory neuron, isolate synaptic storage of A and B, or decisively exclude every alternative form of vector computation.

slides.title: A shortcut does not uniquely establish a cognitive map
body: A **metric cognitive map** represents spatial relationships among familiar places in a common coordinate system. Novel shortcutting is often treated as evidence for such a map, but the same behavior can sometimes follow from simpler stored vectors and continuous self-motion updating.

Cataglyphis ants trained separately to feeders 4.5 m and 5.7 m from the nest searched along their previously untraveled connecting route. The controlled A-to-B test demonstrated flexible navigation toward a second goal without requiring prior experience of that particular route.

The finding makes shortcutting insufficient as a unique diagnostic of map-based navigation. It does not prove that ants can never form other spatial representations; it specifies that this observed behavior is compatible with a nest-referenced vector system and does not require the stronger explanation.
